overview.intro: Every Indian State has a legislature that makes laws for the state. Some states have one House (unicameral) while others have two (bicameral). This chapter explains the Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) and the Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad), their composition, membership qualifications, terms, and their powers and functions.

blocks.text: India is a federal union in which states have their own governments and legislatures. The framers let each state choose whether it needs one House or two: populous states benefit from a directly elected popular House, while a second chamber of experienced members can revise legislation and represent special interests such as teachers, graduates and local bodies. Parliament may create or abolish a Legislative Council in a state if the state Assembly passes a resolution to that effect (Article 169). Today only six states - Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh - retain a Council.

Unicameral and bicameral legislatures. A unicameral legislature has a single House, the Legislative Assembly; a bicameral legislature has two, the Assembly and the Council. The choice depends on the state's needs - the Council adds an examining chamber but slows law-making. A Council may be created or abolished by Parliament when the Assembly of that state passes a resolution by a special majority.

Legislative Assembly - composition. The Assembly is the Lower and popular House. Its members are chosen by direct election on the basis of universal adult franchise from territorial constituencies. The normal strength is not more than 500 and not less than 60 members, though tiny states may have fewer by exception. Some seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. One member is elected by the Assembly as its Speaker, who presides and keeps order.

Legislative Assembly - term and qualifications. The Assembly's normal term is five years, though it can be dissolved earlier, and its term can be extended during a national emergency. To be an MLA a person must be a citizen of India, at least 25 years old, possess the qualifications prescribed by Parliament (and be an elector for an Assembly constituency), and must not hold an office of profit under the government.

Legislative Council - composition. The Council is the Upper House; its strength must not exceed one-third of the Assembly's membership. Members are chosen through multiple channels: one-third are elected by local bodies such as municipalities and district boards; one-twelfth by graduates; one-twelfth by teachers; one-third by MLAs; and the remaining one-sixth are nominated by the Governor from persons distinguished in literature, science, art, cooperative movement and social service.

Legislative Council - term and qualifications. The Council is a permanent House: one-third of its members retire every two years, and each member serves a six-year term. It is never dissolved as a whole. An MLC must be a citizen of India, at least 30 years old, and must satisfy the other qualifications prescribed by Parliament; like MLAs, members must not hold offices of profit. The Council elects its own Chairman, the presiding officer.

Powers and functions of the State Legislature. The State Legislature makes laws on State List subjects (police, public health, agriculture, local government) and on Concurrent List subjects when Parliament permits. It controls the state's finances: no tax can be levied and no money spent without its approval, and the annual budget is presented to the Assembly. It holds the state executive accountable through questions, motions and no-confidence motions. It participates in electing the President and in amending the Constitution, and the Assembly alone can remove the state ministry by a no-confidence vote.

Position of the Legislative Council. The Assembly is the more powerful House. In ordinary legislation the Council can only delay a Bill: the Assembly may ultimately pass it after a waiting period. The Council has no say in votes of no-confidence against the ministry, and in money matters the Assembly's will prevails - the Council may make recommendations which the Assembly may accept or reject. The Council acts mainly as a revising chamber of experienced members.

items: Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) - Popular Lower House; directly elected; five-year term; presided over by the Speaker.
Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) - Upper House in six states; partly elected, partly nominated; permanent house with six-year staggered terms.
Governor - Summons, prorogues and dissolves the Assembly; nominates one-sixth of Council members; assents to Bills.

blocks.text: Legislative Assembly vs Legislative Council: Directly elected popular House with a five-year term versus a permanent, partly elected House with six-year staggered terms.
Unicameral vs Bicameral: One House only (most states) versus two Houses (Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh).
Money Bill vs Ordinary Bill: Can originate only in the Assembly, where the Council cannot veto it, versus may originate in either House of a bicameral state.

items: 1950 - The Constitution comes into force; states organised with Assemblies, some with Councils.
1980s - Several states abolish their Councils as legislative workloads change.
Article 169 in force throughout - Parliament may create or abolish a state Council on the Assembly's resolution.
Recent years - Six states retain Councils: Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh.
Normal term of the Legislative Assembly: 5 years
Term of an MLC: 6 years, one-third retiring every 2 years
Minimum age: 25 years for MLA, 30 years for MLC
State capitals - seat of each Vidhan Sabha / Vidhan Parishad

blocks.text: Cause: Need for a popular House answerable to voters Effect: The Assembly is directly elected by universal adult franchise.
Cause: Desire for a revising chamber of experienced members Effect: Legislative Councils with graduate, teacher and local-body representation were provided.
Cause: A state Assembly resolving by special majority Effect: Parliament may create or abolish that state's Legislative Council (Article 169).
Cause: Money Bills need speedy passage Effect: The Council cannot hold up money legislation; the Assembly's decision prevails.

items: Swapping the minimum ages: MLA is 25, MLC is 30.
Saying the Council can be dissolved - it is a permanent House; only one-third retires every two years.
Writing that the Council has equal power to the Assembly - the Assembly is supreme, especially on money Bills.
Confusing the Speaker (Assembly) with the Chairman (Council).
Listing Local Self-Government as part of the Class IX syllabus - the current unit is The State Legislatures.

keyPoints: Unicameral = Assembly only; bicameral = Assembly + Council.
Assembly: direct, 5 yrs, 25 yrs age, Speaker, 60-500 members.
Council: permanent, 6 yrs, 30 yrs age, Chairman, 1/3 of Assembly strength.
Council mix: 1/3 local bodies + 1/12 grads + 1/12 teachers + 1/3 MLAs + 1/6 nominees.
Assembly supreme: money, ministry removal; Council revises and delays.
examFocus: Assembly: max 500, min 60 members (special cases allowed); term 5 years; age 25; Speaker presides.
Council: cannot exceed one-third of the Assembly; permanent House; term 6 years; age 30; Chairman presides.
Council composition: 1/3 local bodies, 1/12 graduates, 1/12 teachers, 1/3 MLAs, 1/6 Governor's nominees.
The Council can delay ordinary Bills but cannot amend Money Bills or reject the ministry.
Article 169: creation or abolition of a Council on the state Assembly's resolution.
States with Councils today: Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh.
The state Legislature controls the State List and sanctions all state taxation and spending.

A legislature with two Houses - the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council.
The popular House of a State Legislature, directly elected by the people for five years.
The permanent, indirectly elected upper House of a State Legislature, which can never be fully dissolved.

questions.prompt: Which of these states currently has a Legislative Council?
questions.explanation: Only six states have Councils: Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming large states like Tamil Nadu have Councils.

questions.prompt: The minimum age to become a member of the Legislative Assembly is:
questions.commonMistake: Swapping the ages for the two Houses.

questions.prompt: The strength of a Legislative Council cannot exceed:
questions.explanation: The Council is the smaller, revising chamber - max one-third of the Assembly's strength.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming the Council can be as large as the Assembly.

questions.prompt: Who presides over the Legislative Assembly?
questions.answer: The Speaker, elected by the Assembly from among its members.
questions.explanation: The Council's presiding officer is the Chairman.

questions.prompt: What fraction of Council members retires every two years?
questions.explanation: That staggered retirement is why the Council is called a permanent House.
questions.commonMistake: Saying one-half or that all retire together.

questions.prompt: State the qualifications for membership of the Legislative Assembly.
questions.answer: The person must be a citizen of India; at least 25 years old; possess qualifications prescribed by Parliament (including being an elector for an Assembly constituency); and must not hold an office of profit under the government.
questions.explanation: Citizenship, age, electorship and no office of profit.

questions.prompt: How is the Legislative Council composed?
questions.answer: One-third elected by local bodies (municipalities, district boards); one-twelfth by graduates; one-twelfth by teachers; one-third by MLAs; and one-sixth nominated by the Governor from distinguished persons in literature, science, art, the cooperative movement and social service.

questions.prompt: What are the powers of the State Legislature over money matters?
questions.answer: No tax can be imposed and no money spent by the state government without the Legislature's sanction; the annual budget (financial statement) is placed before the Assembly; Money Bills can originate only in the Assembly, and the Council can only make recommendations which the Assembly may accept or reject within a fixed period.
questions.explanation: Financial control is the legislature's core check on the executive.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the Council can veto Money Bills.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council.
questions.answer: The Assembly is the popular Lower House: directly elected by universal adult franchise, normal term five years (may be dissolved earlier), minimum age 25, presided over by the Speaker, and the powerful House on money and confidence matters. The Council is the Upper House: never more than one-third of the Assembly, a permanent House with one-third of members retiring every two years for a six-year term, minimum age 30, presided over by a Chairman, chosen through five channels (local bodies, graduates, teachers, MLAs, Governor's nominees). The Assembly decides who governs; the Council mainly revises and delays ordinary legislation.
questions.explanation: Composition, term, age, presiding officer and power contrast.
questions.commonMistake: Missing the 'permanent House' nature of the Council.

questions.prompt: Give reasons: The Legislative Council is called a permanent body.
questions.answer: It is never dissolved as a whole. Like the Rajya Sabha, one-third of its members retire every two years while others continue, so the House always exists. This continuity lets it revise legislation without the disruption of general dissolution - hence 'permanent'.

questions.prompt: Explain the powers and functions of the State Legislature.
questions.answer: Legislative: makes laws on State List subjects (public order, police, public health, agriculture, local government) and on Concurrent subjects where permitted; in bicameral states, ordinary Bills pass both Houses, but the Assembly's will ultimately prevails. Financial: no tax without its sanction; the budget is presented to it; Money Bills originate only in the Assembly, and the Council's recommendations can be overridden. Executive control: ministers are responsible to the Assembly, which questions them (question hour), moves motions, and can remove the ministry through a no-confidence motion - the Council cannot. Electoral: the elected members take part in electing the President; Assemblies also elect Rajya Sabha and Council members. Constitutional: the Legislature ratifies constitutional amendments referred to states, and under Article 169 can resolve to create or abolish its own Council. Thus the State Legislature makes law, controls finance, checks the executive and shares in national constitutional processes.
questions.explanation: Cover legislative, financial, control, electoral and constitutional functions.

questions.prompt: A bicameral state's Assembly passes a Money Bill; the Council delays it for months. What happens, and why?
questions.answer: The Council can only make recommendations for a fixed period; after that, the Assembly may pass the Bill and send it for the Governor's assent regardless. Money Bills originate in the Assembly and the Council has no veto over them, because financial responsibility rests with the popular House whose members sanction the state's spending.
questions.explanation: Apply the Money Bill procedure to the scenario.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the Council's delay blocks the Bill indefinitely.
